slides: Open by presenting the chapter as a classification problem with pictures attached. The students should hear that a quadratic form is not just a polynomial, but a measurement rule whose level sets reveal signature, radical, and isotropy. Point to the cone motif and preview that the same algebra will later drive projective quadrics.

Spend time on the cross term. The coefficient of x1 x2 appears twice in x transpose A x, once from each off-diagonal position, so the symmetric matrix is not bookkeeping trivia. Then derive polarization aloud as the operation that turns level-set intuition into the orthogonality relation used for radicals and reflections.

Contrast congruence with the more familiar similarity transformation without turning the slide into a side lecture. The key is that a quadratic form eats one vector twice, so changing coordinates introduces P transpose on the left and P on the right. The classifying information is therefore the inertia, not the raw eigenvalue list under arbitrary congruence.

Use the artifact as a diagnostic exercise rather than a display to admire. Ask the room to predict the signature before naming each panel. The red zero set is the anchor: a point for definite forms, crossing lines for a nondegenerate indefinite form, and a full forgotten direction for the rank-one semidefinite form.

This is the conceptual fork students need before projective quadrics. A radical direction is invisible to the entire bilinear form, while an isotropic direction in a nondegenerate indefinite plane is visible because it pairs with another direction. Keep returning to the phrase zero for different reasons, since the later quotient step depends on it.

Use the Lorentz cone as the smallest spatial model where the words cone, sign, and component all become literal. The point is not special relativity; it is that the same quadratic form partitions space into positive, negative, and isotropic zones. Invite students to rotate the linked artifact later to see that no coordinate slice tells the whole story.

This slide is the formal payoff for the previous visual diagnostics. The heatmap should be read left to right: mixed coordinates make every direction communicate, while orthogonal coordinates separate the signs and expose the radical. Emphasize that the zero slot survives because it is a structural radical direction, not a rounding artifact.

Give the class a proof map without burying them in computations. The induction idea is to find one direction the form sees, remove all directions paired with it, and repeat. If the process reaches invisible directions, those are radical. If it reaches isotropic directions that still pair with each other, the next slide names the hyperbolic plane.

The hyperbolic plane is the moment where isotropic directions become constructive. Stress that e and f each have zero value, yet neither is invisible because B of e and f is nonzero. Changing to e plus f and e minus f recovers one positive and one negative square, explaining why Witt decomposition is just inertia organized into paired geometry.

Connect the formula to the earlier polar form. A reflection is not guessed from the picture; it is forced by the requirement to flip v while fixing every vector B-orthogonal to v. In indefinite signature the picture looks unfamiliar, but the same preservation calculation keeps every point on the same quadratic level.

Treat this as the student-facing algorithm for the chapter. The checklist starts with symmetrization because many raw matrices in computation are not presented politely. Once the signature and radical are known, every later decision becomes local: whether to draw a cone, quotient a radical, find hyperbolic planes, or test a proposed symmetry.

Close by separating the durable ideas from the computational decorations. Students should leave knowing that the entries of a quadratic matrix are negotiable, but the inertia and radical are not. The zero set is a diagnostic, not a single phenomenon. Reflections then show that the polar form also generates motion, preparing the transition to quadrics.
